events.description: Narrow Politburo group meets in Brezhnev's office, weighs pros and cons of troops, and orders two options developed: remove Amin via KGB, or send troops.

Ustinov informs Ogarkov of preliminary decision and orders 75-80 thousand troops prepared; Ogarkov objects; small Politburo session tentatively agrees to prepare troops; Ministry of Defense Collegium convened, Directive 312/12/00133 sent.
Ustinov summons Zaplatin to Moscow to report on the Afghan army.
Politburo unanimously decides to introduce Soviet troops into Afghanistan, termed 'the measures'; protocol handwritten by Chernenko; Kosygin absent.
Narrow Politburo meeting in Brezhnev's office discussing introducing Soviet troops; decided to develop two options (remove Amin via KGB, or send troops).
Ustinov summoned Ogarkov, informed him of preliminary decision and ordered preparation of 75-80 thousand troops; Ogarkov objected.
Ogarkov summoned to Brezhnev's office where the 'small Politburo' decided to prepare troops without final decision.
Ustinov gathered the Ministry of Defense Collegium; Directive #312/12/00133 sent to troops; formation of a new army in Turkestan Military District begun.
Ustinov summoned Zaplatin to Moscow to report on the Afghan army.
Politburo session unanimously decided to introduce Soviet troops into Afghanistan, termed 'the measures'; protocol handwritten by Chernenko.
KGB representative B. Ivanov in Kabul sent report/coded telegram assessing the Afghan situation, influencing the final decision.

key_claims: The Politburo's narrow group (Andropov, Ustinov, Gromyko) initiated the 12 Dec 1979 decision to send troops into Afghanistan.
Options considered on 8 Dec were removing Amin via KGB and installing Babrak Karmal, or sending troops.
Justifications cited included alleged CIA plans, Pershing missiles in Afghanistan, Afghan uranium use by Pakistan and Iraq, and Pakistani annexation of northern Afghanistan.
Ogarkov opposed the move as reckless and favored political means but was overruled by Ustinov.
The KGB representative Ivanov's alarming report was the final push, over Zaplatin's objection that special services dramatized the situation.
No formal state decree was issued; all orders were oral to preserve secrecy and mislead Amin.
